overview: This bill aims to stop people and businesses from being taxed twice, by both the United States and Taiwan, on the same income. Because of Taiwan's unique diplomatic status, the U.S. cannot sign a regular tax treaty with it, so the bill writes similar benefits directly into the federal tax code. For qualifying Taiwan residents, it lowers the standard 30 percent U.S. tax withheld on interest, royalties, and similar payments to 10 percent, and on dividends to 15 percent (10 percent for larger corporate shareholders); it also exempts certain wages and taxes business profits only when tied to a fixed U.S. place of business. These benefits apply only if the Treasury Department finds Taiwan gives matching benefits to Americans, and the bill includes rules to keep companies from other countries from abusing them. It also authorizes the President to negotiate a fuller tax agreement with Taiwan, with consultation and approval by Congress. The House passed it, and as of January 16, 2025, it had been sent to the Senate Finance Committee.
for: Supporters say ending double taxation will encourage investment and trade between the U.S. and Taiwan, a major economic partner, and put Taiwan on similar footing to countries that have tax treaties.
against: Critics say the lower withholding rates mean less U.S. tax revenue, and that writing treaty-like terms into law outside the normal treaty process sets a complicated precedent.
